title: Getting Started with Rezure
excerpt: Set up your local development environment on Windows in under five minutes — Nginx, PHP, and MariaDB running with a single click.
content:
Rezure turns a fresh Windows install into a working web-development machine in about two minutes. No manual downloads, no editing config files by hand, no "which PHP version did I install?" confusion.

What you get out of the box

The installer bundles Nginx 1.27 and PHP 8.3, so serving a site works the moment setup finishes. MariaDB is pulled on demand the first time you need a database — one click inside the app and it is ready.

First steps

  1. Download the installer from the download page and run it.
  2. Launch Rezure — the service manager opens automatically.
  3. Start Nginx and PHP-FPM with a single click. The status indicators turn green when the services are healthy.
  4. Drop a project into your working folder. Rezure generates the Nginx vhost config and updates your Windows hosts file for you.

Next up

Once the stack is running you can share a project publicly through a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel, pin a PHP version per project, or connect to a remote database through an SSH tunnel — all from the same window.

title: Switching PHP Versions Per Project
excerpt: Run PHP 7.4 for a legacy app and PHP 8.3 for a new one at the same time — Rezure handles the routing automatically.
content:
Not every project can jump to the latest PHP overnight. A client site might still need 7.4, while your new API targets 8.3. Rezure lets each project declare which PHP version it wants, and spins up a dedicated php-cgi process for it.

How it works

Rezure scans your download cache and a drop-in folder for installed PHP builds. The installable list comes live from php.net's own release feed, checksums included, so you always know you are running an official build.

Setting a version for a project

  1. Open the project settings in Rezure.
  2. Pick the PHP version from the dropdown — if it is not installed yet, Rezure downloads it for you.
  3. Restart the project's virtual host. Rezure starts a php-cgi instance on a dedicated port and points Nginx at it.

Running side by side

Because each project gets its own php-cgi process, two projects on different PHP versions run at the same time without conflict. Switch between them in your browser and the right PHP handles each request.

title: Why We Built Rezure with Tauri and Rust
excerpt: A look behind the curtain — why a desktop app for web developers is written in Rust, and how Tauri keeps it small and fast.
content:
When we started Rezure the first prototype was an Electron app. It worked, but the installer was over 150 MB and idle RAM sat around 300 MB — for a tool that is supposed to stay in the background while you code. That did not feel right.

Enter Tauri

Tauri uses the operating system's built-in WebView instead of shipping a full Chromium browser. On Windows 10 and 11 that means Microsoft Edge WebView2, which is already installed on almost every machine. The result: a ~8 MB installer and ~40 MB of RAM at idle.

Why Rust matters

The backend of a Tauri app is plain Rust. For Rezure that means:

  • Process management — starting, stopping, and monitoring Nginx, PHP-FPM, and MariaDB is handled by safe, compiled code with no garbage-collector pauses.
  • Port scanning — checking whether port 80 or 3306 is already taken happens in microseconds.
  • File I/O — generating Nginx configs and editing the Windows hosts file is fast and predictable.

The trade-off

Rust has a steep learning curve and compile times are longer than TypeScript's hot reload. But for a system-level tool that users leave running all day, the performance and memory savings are worth it.
